Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the model forecasts compared to true outcomes, while considering sentiment history.

## Example 1 Analysis (2025-04-10)
History: Price dropped from 70+ to 60- range over 18 days (roughly 15% drop)
Sentiment: Mixed, ending at 0.00
Model forecasts: Started at 62.35, gradually increasing to ~67 by day 30
True outcomes: Started at 62.12, but increased MORE than forecasts, ending around 71.56 (about 3-4% above model's highest forecast of 67.19)

The model was too conservative on the upside. The prices continued to rise beyond what the model projected.

## Example 2 Analysis (2024-05-01)
History: Price in 66-74 range, no clear trend
Sentiment: Mostly positive (0.33+)
Model forecasts: Around 68-73 range
True outcomes: Around 67.91-76.67 range - about 2-4% higher than model

Again, model under-forecasted prices, especially on the upside.

## Example 3 Analysis (2024-04-09)
This is essentially the same as Example 1 but at a different timestamp.
History is identical (just shifted one day)
Sentiment is identical
Model forecasts are very similar (61.48 vs 62.35 on day 1)
True outcomes are identical (60.94 vs 62.12 on day 1)

So Examples 1 and 3 show the same error pattern.

## Example 4 Analysis (2024-05-02)
History: Similar to Example 2
Sentiment: Similar to Example 2
Model forecasts: Around 72.92-71.33 on day 1-30


True outcomes: 72.69-70.30 - about 2-4% below model forecasts this time!

I notice a fascinating reversal in the model's forecasting performance. Previously under-forecasting prices, the model now seems to be overestimating values, particularly at the beginning of the 30-day horizon. The consistent 2-4% variations suggest a systematic bias in the original forecasting approach.

The sentiment history reveals an interesting progression from initial uncertainty (0.00) to increasing confidence (0.50, 1.00), which might correlate with the model's shifting predictions.
